sections.title: *Magbiah Metziah La'chavero*: Fails (Rav Nachman) or Works (R. Yochanan)?
sections.gist: Continuing the question of whether lifting a find for another acquires it for him: the Mishnah's word 'at the outset', Rav Nachman's creditor analogy, Rava's objection from the hired laborer, and R. Yochanan's contrary view.

chart.caption: Lifting a find for another: three views, and how each reads the rider Mishnah
columns: Why the Mishnah's lifter may keep it
rows: Ulla
Yes: for a find, everyone is like a poor man, and he could take it himself
He says he meant it for himself at the outset
When it is lifted, if lifted for him
Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda
No: *tofes le'ba'al chov be'makom she'chav le'acherim*
Even without claiming he meant it for himself
Only when it is handed to him
R. Chiya bar Abba citing R. Yochanan
Yes
The rider said "give it to me", not "acquire it for me"
At the lifting if he said "acquire it for me"; on receipt if "give it to me"

children.title: 'At the Outset': Did the Lifter Claim He Took It for Himself?
children.gist: The last clause's word 'at the outset' supports Ulla's reading of the first clause; Rav Nachman reads the same word as a contrast with it.

bullets.text: The Mishnah's last clause: if, after handing the find to the rider, the lifter says "I acquired it for myself at the outset", his words count for nothing. Why say "at the outset"? That is obviously what he means.
So the word must be there to teach about the first clause: there too the lifter keeps the find because he says he meant it for himself from the outset. This supports Ulla's reading.

Rav Nachman: the last clause says "at the outset" to shed light on the first by contrast. There the lifter keeps it even if he makes no such claim, since the rider acquires nothing until it is given to him.

The stakes: on Ulla's reading, lifting for another works, so a lifter who took it for the rider could not change his mind. On Rav Nachman's, the act never works, so until he hands it over only the lifter can own it.

How can intent outweigh a physical lift of an ownerless object? Acquisition is always an act plus intent. Even a *chatzer* acquiring without the owner's knowledge rests on a presumption that he wants the item, and explicit contrary intent can override a presumption.

children.title: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: It Fails, Like *Tofes Le'ba'al Chov*
children.gist: Seizing a debtor's assets for one creditor at the other creditors' expense doesn't acquire, and lifting a find for one person deprives everyone else in the same way.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: in *magbiah metziah la'chavero*, lifting a find on behalf of another, the other does not acquire it.

The reason: it is *tofes le'ba'al chov be'makom she'chav le'acherim*. One who seizes a debtor's assets for one creditor when others are owed too does not acquire for him. Everyone has an equal right to an ownerless find, so no one can take that right from all the others for one person.

Tosafot: one could hold that seizing for a creditor fails and still hold that lifting a find for another works. A bystander has no claim on the debtor's assets, but the finder could have kept the find himself (*migo de'zakhi le'nafshei*).
A further difference, not the one Tosafot draw: the other creditors lose money really owed to them, while other would-be finders lose only a windfall.

Rashi holds that formally appointing an agent would change the outcome; Tosafot disagree, since an appointment gives no right to cut off others. The Mishnah's rider, who in effect sends the pedestrian, suggests that even agency may not help.

Rabbeinu Tam: drawing water for another from a public well raises no such problem, since plenty is left and no one is harmed. And if the mechanism is the *migo*, the drawer is seen as acquiring for himself and then passing it on, so for *eiruvin* the water's *techum* follows the one who drew it.

children.title: Rava's Objection: The Laborer's Find and *Yado Ke'yad Ba'al Ha'bayit*
children.gist: Two steps: a baraita gives a laborer's find to his employer, which Rav Nachman explains by the laborer's hand being the employer's, and he defends that against the laborer's right to quit.

children.title: 'Weed for Me' or 'Work for Me': Whose Is the Laborer's Find?
children.gist: A laborer hired for a set task keeps his find, while one hired for any work finds for his employer; Rav Nachman answers that a laborer is different because his hand is the employer's.

bullets.text: Rava objects from a baraita: a laborer's find belongs to him. When? When the employer said "weed for me today" or "till for me today".
But if he said "work for me today", the find is the employer's, since finding is included in work. So a laborer can acquire for someone else, against Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman: a laborer is different. *Yado ke'yad ba'al ha'bayit*: his hand is like the employer's hand while he works for him.

With a set task, lifting the find is outside the job; at most the employer can claim the few minutes lost. With an open-ended hire the whole day is contracted, so the laborer's act is the employer's act. This is a contractual bond, more than agency.

children.title: Quitting at Midday: 'My Slaves, Not Slaves of Slaves'
children.gist: Rava asks how a laborer's hand can be his employer's if he may quit at midday; Rav Nachman answers that it is until he quits, and the right to quit rests on Vayikra 25:55.

bullets.text: Rava: but Rav says a laborer may quit even at midday. Doesn't that show the arrangement favors the laborer, so his hand is not the employer's?

Rav Nachman: as long as he hasn't quit, his hand is the employer's. His right to quit has a different source: "For to Me the children of Israel are slaves" (Vayikra 25:55). They are My slaves, not slaves of slaves.

The Gemara doesn't let the principle against servitude cancel *yado ke'yad ba'al ha'bayit*. While he works the laborer really is an extension of his employer; the guaranteed right to leave keeps that bond from hardening into servitude.
Tosafot: the laborer also holds the upper hand in any renegotiation over the rest of the day.
Tosafot: a person is permitted to hire himself out. What is excluded is *avdut*, as with an *eved Ivri*, who cannot leave before his term ends. The right to quit keeps ordinary employment permitted.
The Gra cites the Hagahot Maimoniyot: it is forbidden to hire oneself out for more than three years, since so long a commitment comes close to servitude.

children.title: R. Yochanan: It Works; 'Give It to Me' Isn't 'Acquire It for Me'
children.gist: R. Chiya bar Abba in R. Yochanan's name: lifting a find for another acquires it for him, and the Mishnah's rider only asked to have it handed to him.

bullets.text: R. Chiya bar Abba, citing R. Yochanan, disagrees with Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda: one who lifts a find for another acquires it for him.

The Mishnah is a case where the rider said "give it to me", not "acquire it for me". Then he acquires only once it reaches his possession. Had he said "acquire it for me", he would acquire it as soon as the pedestrian lifted it.
Delivering and acquiring are different acts. Asked only to deliver, the pedestrian lifts the find with no intent to vest title in the rider, so he may still change his mind before handing it over.

The result is three ways to explain the Mishnah's lifter: the act never works (Rav Nachman); it works, but he says he meant it for himself at the outset (Ulla); or it works, but he was asked only to deliver (R. Yochanan).

sections.title: Mishnah: Falling on a Find vs. Seizing It; *Arba Amot* and Its Limits
sections.gist: One who falls on a find loses it to one who seizes it; the Gemara adds Reish Lakish's rule that a person's *arba amot* acquire for him, then answers objections from Pe'ah and from this Mishnah, with Rav Pappa and Rav Sheshet limiting where it applies.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one who saw a find and fell on it, and another came and seized it: the one who seized it acquires it.
Falling on an object, however complete the bodily contact, is no act of acquisition. Acquiring needs an act of taking possession, such as lifting or drawing the item.

chart.caption: Two objections to *arba amot*, each with the shared answer and its own alternative answer
rows: Pe'ah 4:3 (R. Chiya bar Yosef, reported by Abaye)
A poor man throws gleanings on the *pe'ah*, falls on it or spreads his garment over it: he gets nothing of it
By falling he showed he wanted to acquire by falling, not by *arba amot*
Rav Pappa: *arba amot* don't acquire in an owner's field
Our Mishnah, in *Nezikin* (R. Ya'akov bar Idi, reported by Rava)
One falls on a find and another seizes it: the one who seized it acquires
The same: falling revealed which mode of acquisition he chose
Rav Sheshet: *arba amot* don't acquire in the crowded public domain

children.title: Reish Lakish: *Arba Amot* Acquire Everywhere, to Prevent Quarrels
children.gist: In Abba Kohen Bardela's name, a person's four cubits acquire ownerless items for him like his *chatzer*, a rabbinic enactment against fighting, and two objections are announced against it.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish, citing Abba Kohen Bardela: *arba amot shel adam konot lo be'khol makom*. The four cubits around a person have the status of his *chatzer* and acquire any ownerless item in them for him, everywhere.
The reason: the Sages enacted it so that people would not come to quarrel over a find.
Abaye reports an objection by R. Chiya bar Yosef from a Mishnah in Pe'ah; Rava reports one by R. Ya'akov bar Idi from a Mishnah in *Nezikin*.
*Arba amot* work as a portable personal domain. They settle priority by closeness and end the race before people scramble for the item itself. The rule is used mainly for finds and for a *get*.

children.title: The Pe'ah Objection: Falling on *Pe'ah*, Choice of Mode, or Owner's Field?
children.gist: The Mishnah in Pe'ah gives nothing to a poor man who fell on *pe'ah*; the Gemara answers that falling showed he didn't want his *arba amot*, and Rav Pappa that the enactment doesn't apply in an owner's field.

bullets.text: Pe'ah 4:3: a poor man who took some *pe'ah* and threw it on the rest, fell on it or spread his garment over it gets none of it; others may remove him. The same holds for a forgotten sheaf.
R. Chiya bar Yosef: if *arba amot* acquire everywhere, his should acquire the *pe'ah* for him.

Tosafot: the one who takes the *pe'ah* out from under him is not even called a *rasha*. The rule of *ani ha'mehapekh be'charara*, that snatching what another is pursuing makes one a *rasha*, doesn't apply to an ownerless item, since the snatcher can't be told to find another like it elsewhere.

children.title: He Fell on It: Choosing Falling over *Arba Amot*
children.gist: The problem isn't that he never said 'I will acquire'; by falling he showed he meant to acquire by falling, not by his *arba amot*.

bullets.text: First answer: he didn't say "I will acquire it".
Rejected: if the Sages enacted *arba amot*, why should he need to say anything?
Rather: by falling on it he showed that he wanted to acquire by falling and not by his *arba amot*. Falling is no mode of acquisition, so he acquired nothing.

*Arba amot* are not automatic; a mode of acquisition the person chooses displaces them. Compare one who means to acquire a cup by lifting (*hagbahah*) but raises it less than three handbreadths, and so has in fact drawn it (*meshikhah*): does the failed act he chose block the valid one?

children.title: Rav Pappa: *Arba Amot* Don't Work in an Owner's Field
children.gist: The enactment applies on public land; the Torah gave the poor a right to walk and glean in an owner's field, not to treat it as their *chatzer*.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: the Sages enacted *arba amot* "in the world", on public land, not in a field that has an owner.
The Torah gave the poor the right to walk in the field and collect *pe'ah*, but not the right to have the field count as their *chatzer*. So the Mishnah in Pe'ah is no objection.

*Arba amot* are a kind of portable *chatzer*, and a visitor's personal space can't override the owner's actual domain. On neutral ground neither claimant has the stronger claim, so *arba amot* can work.

children.title: The *Nezikin* Objection: Our Mishnah, and Rav Sheshet's Alleyway
children.gist: The same objection from this Mishnah gets the same answer, and Rav Sheshet limits *arba amot* to an alleyway, not the crowded public domain, reading 'everywhere' as the sides of the public domain.

children.title: Our Mishnah: The Same Objection and the Same Answer
children.gist: Why doesn't the one who fell on the find acquire it by his *arba amot*? Because by falling he showed he didn't want them.

bullets.text: R. Ya'akov bar Idi: in our Mishnah, the one who fell on the find should have acquired it through his *arba amot*.

The same sequence as before: not because he didn't say "I will acquire it", since the enactment needs no words, but because falling revealed that he chose to acquire by falling and not by his *arba amot*.

returns_to.note: Repeats the answer given to the Pe'ah objection

children.title: Rav Sheshet: An Alleyway, Not the Crowded Public Domain
children.gist: *Arba amot* were enacted where crowds don't press; Reish Lakish's 'everywhere' only adds the sides of the public domain.

bullets.text: Rav Sheshet: the Sages enacted *arba amot* for a place like an alleyway, where crowds don't press, not for the public domain, where they do.
Challenge: Reish Lakish said "everywhere". Answer: the word isn't literal; it adds the sides of the public domain, where crowds don't press.
In a crowd, personal space disappears, so the rule has nothing to rest on. Compare the rule that drawing an item (*meshikhah*) acquires in an alleyway but not in the public domain.

sections.title: Minor Girl's *Chatzer* and *Arba Amot*: Hand or Agency?
sections.gist: Reish Lakish and R. Yochanan dispute whether a minor girl acquires by *chatzer* and *arba amot*, framed as *chatzer* as her hand or as her agent; the agency view is then tested against theft through a *chatzer*, answered by Ravina and Rav Samma.
sections.continues: Continues on 10b: the practical difference between Ravina and Rav Samma (a kohen who sends an Israelite to betroth a divorcée; a man who sends a woman to round a boy's head), then a challenge to Abba Kohen Bardela from the baraita on a *get* placed in a woman's *chatzer*.

children.title: Reish Lakish vs. R. Yochanan: *Chatzer* as Her Hand or Her Agent
children.gist: If a *chatzer* is an extension of her hand, a minor girl has one; if it works as her agent, she doesn't, since a minor can't appoint an agent.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish, citing Abba Kohen Bardela: a minor girl has neither *chatzer* nor *arba amot*. R. Yochanan, citing R. Yannai: she has both.
R. Yannai: *chatzer* was included as a mode of acquisition because it is like her hand. She can acquire with her hand, so she can acquire with her *chatzer*.
Abba Kohen Bardela: *chatzer* was included because of agency (*shelichut*). A minor cannot appoint an agent, so she has no *chatzer* either.
On the agency view there is something almost personal about a *chatzer*: an inanimate property takes possession on its owner's behalf, as an agent would.

Background: a *get* "in her hand" (Devarim 24:1) also works in her *chatzer*, and a minor girl married off by her father can be divorced. *Arba amot* run on the same logic as *chatzer*. Though rabbinic in origin, once enacted they can effect a divorce at the Torah level.

children.title: Theft Through a *Chatzer*: Can There Be *Shelichut* for a Transgression?
children.gist: A baraita makes a thief liable when the stolen item is found in his *chatzer*, which seems to contradict *ein shaliach le'devar aveirah* on the agency view; Ravina and Rav Samma each explain why a *chatzer* is different.

bullets.text: Baraita on Shemot 22:3, "if the theft shall be found in his possession": "in his hand" covers only his hand; the doubled *himatze timatze* adds his roof, his *chatzer* and his enclosure.
If a *chatzer* acquires through agency, this is agency for a transgression, yet the rule is *ein shaliach le'devar aveirah*: one who sends an agent to transgress is not liable; the agent is.

When a human agent steals for his sender, the sender acquires nothing and owes nothing. So on the agency view the owner of the *chatzer* should escape liability, which is exactly what the baraita rules out.

Rav Samma

Items are put in a *chatzer* without its consent, so its owner is liable

children.title: Ravina: Only an Agent Who Is *Bar Chiyuva*; What of a Woman or Slave?
children.gist: The rule shields the sender only when the agent is himself subject to liability, which a *chatzer* is not; a woman or slave counts as liable even without the means to pay.

bullets.text: Ravina: *ein shaliach le'devar aveirah* applies where the agent is himself subject to liability (*bar chiyuva*), so the agent is liable and not the sender. A *chatzer* is not subject to liability, so its owner is.
Challenge: then one who tells a woman or a slave "go out and steal for me" should be liable, since they have no property to pay from.
Answer: a woman and a slave are subject to liability; they just can't pay now. Bava Kamma 87a: if a woman who caused an injury is divorced, or a slave who did is freed, they must pay.

Behind the rule: when the master's words and the student's words conflict, whose does one obey? The agent should have obeyed God, so the choice and the responsibility are his. A *chatzer* receives no command and makes no choice.

children.title: Rav Samma: Only an Agent Who Could Refuse (*I Ba'i Avid*)
children.gist: The rule shields the sender only when the agent is free to act or refuse; items are put in a *chatzer* without its consent, so its owner is liable.

bullets.text: Rav Samma: *ein shaliach le'devar aveirah* applies where the agent can carry out the task if he wants and refrain if he wants (*i ba'i avid, i ba'i lo avid*). Items are put in a *chatzer* without its consent, so its owner is liable.
Even on the agency view, a *chatzer* is an agent without will. It acts for its owner but cannot take on responsibility, so here there is, in effect, agency even for a transgression.

key_terms.sense: lifting an ownerless find on behalf of another
key_terms.definition: The question of whether one who performs an act of acquisition on an ownerless item with intent that another person acquire it thereby makes that other person its owner.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda say the other does not acquire; R. Yochanan says he does, and each side reads the rider Mishnah to fit.

key_terms.term: tofes le'ba'al chov be'makom she'chav le'acherim
key_terms.hebrew: תופס לבעל חוב במקום שחב לאחרים
key_terms.sense: seizing for one creditor at others' expense
key_terms.definition: The rule that a third party who seizes a debtor's assets on behalf of one creditor, where this harms other creditors, does not acquire them for that creditor.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda compare lifting a find for another to it, since it cuts off everyone else's equal right to the find.
aliases: tofes le'ba'al chov be'makom she'chav le'acherim

key_terms.sense: a hired worker's hand as his employer's
key_terms.definition: The principle that while a hired worker is employed, his acts in the course of the work count as his employer's, so what he acquires in that capacity belongs to the employer.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Nachman uses it to explain why a laborer hired for any work finds for his employer, and holds that it lasts until the laborer quits.

key_terms.sense: acquisition by the four cubits around a person
key_terms.definition: A rabbinic enactment under which the four cubits surrounding a person acquire for him an ownerless item that lies within them, as his courtyard would.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Reish Lakish states it in Abba Kohen Bardela's name; the Gemara explains why it fails for one who fell on a find, and Rav Pappa and Rav Sheshet exclude an owner's field and the crowded public domain.
aliases: arba amot shel adam konot lo be'khol makom

key_terms.definition: A person's courtyard or other property acquires for him items that enter it, even without his own act of taking possession.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yannai grounds it in the owner's hand and Abba Kohen Bardela in agency, which decides whether a minor girl has one; the agency view is then tested by theft through a *chatzer*.

key_terms.definition: The rule that when one sends an agent to commit a transgression, the act is not attributed to the sender; the agent bears the liability.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It seems to contradict a thief's liability for a stolen item found in his *chatzer*; Ravina and Rav Samma each limit the rule so that it doesn't cover a *chatzer*.

key_terms.definition: A person who is himself bound by a prohibition and liable for violating it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: For Ravina, only an agent who is *bar chiyuva* shields his sender; a woman or slave counts as one even without the means to pay, while a *chatzer* does not.

judgment_calls: The 'at the outset' exchange (10a.3–4) is the tail of the Ulla–Rav Nachman debate from 9b; placed it as the first child of the larger question of lifting for another, instead of a separate top-level section, because it serves the same question that Rav Nachman's and R. Yochanan's rulings then state outright.

The Mishnah of 10a.13 is made the parent of the whole *arba amot* discussion (10a.13–10b.6), since the Gemara's second objection comes from this Mishnah itself. An alternative was a short Mishnah section with *arba amot* as a separate top-level section.

Rav Pappa's answer is nested under the Pe'ah objection and Rav Sheshet's under the *Nezikin* objection, following which objection each 'different answer' in the text is attached to. Grouping the two limits together as one 'where *arba amot* apply' section was also possible; the illustration on the parent brings them together instead.

The minor-girl dispute (10b.7) is a new top-level section rather than a child of *arba amot*. It is another statement of Reish Lakish citing Abba Kohen Bardela, but it turns on the nature of *chatzer*, and the rest of the daf follows that thread.

The theft challenge and the answers of Ravina and Rav Samma are nested under the minor-girl dispute because they test Abba Kohen Bardela's premise that *chatzer* works through agency; they could stand as their own top-level section on *ein shaliach le'devar aveirah*.

Tosafot's point that the one who takes *pe'ah* from under the one who fell isn't a *rasha* is placed with the Pe'ah objection (s10), where the case of being removed from the *pe'ah* is stated, and not in the answer section.
coverage_notes: Lines 10a.1–10a.2 (Rav Nachman's proof from the rider Mishnah and Ulla's reply) belong to the previous daf's outline; the previous shiur's tail covered them. The essay's opening sections on the *migo* principle and on seizing for a creditor restate that background and are used here only where they bear on 10a.3 onward.

The essay presents 'the last clause teaches to shed light on the first' as support for the original-intent reading. In the text, Ulla's support is that 'at the outset' in the last clause must teach about the first clause, and 'to shed light on the first clause' is Rav Nachman's reply, meaning the first clause holds even without that claim. Followed the text.
The essay credits 'Rava' with the second, 'better' answer to the theft challenge. The text gives it to Rav Samma and presents it only as a different resolution. Followed the text.

The essay garbles the minor-girl dispute (it first gives the hand view to Reish Lakish and then corrects itself) and omits the chains of transmission. The text: Reish Lakish citing Abba Kohen Bardela (no *chatzer*, no *arba amot*), and R. Yochanan citing R. Yannai (both); the Gemara assigns the hand rationale to R. Yannai and the agency rationale to Abba Kohen Bardela. Followed the text.
The essay says the Gemara reconciles 'everywhere' with the limits of both Rav Pappa and Rav Sheshet. In the text the 'everywhere' challenge is raised only against Rav Sheshet. Followed the text.

The essay (following the Gra's reading) describes Rav Pappa's setting as a field in which no party has a stronger claim; the translation reads 'in the world, i.e., on public land'. Used the text's wording in Gemara bullets and kept the lecturer's framing as a shiur bullet.
The essay spells the names 'Rav Papa' and 'Rav Sheshes'; the text has Rav Pappa and Rav Sheshet. Followed the text.
The second objection to *arba amot*, R. Ya'akov bar Idi's from our Mishnah (10b.2–3), is named in the segmentation but not discussed in the essay; outlined from the text and flagged.
The essay's account of Tosafot on *ani ha'mehapekh be'charara* mixes in a comparison to land; the outline gives only its main point (a find cannot be sought elsewhere), marked as shiur.
The text from 10b.15 onward (the practical difference between Ravina and Rav Samma, and the challenge from the *get* baraita) falls to the next outline; the essay does not discuss it.
